lesson.title: The Left-Hand Limit: Sneaking Up From Below
lesson.summary: The left-hand limit restricts every test input to values strictly below the target, and the floor function makes a vivid case study where the approach value and the value at the point turn out to be different numbers entirely.
lesson.body:
The left-hand limit is the specific one-sided limit where x is restricted to values strictly less than a, written lim(x to a-) f(x). The small raised minus mark is not a negative sign attached to a; it is a direction marker meaning "approach a from below, using only inputs smaller than a." Every input considered in this limit sits to the left of a on the number line, getting closer and closer without ever reaching or passing it.

A good function for seeing left-hand limits clearly is the floor function, f(x) = floor(x), which rounds any real input down to the nearest integer. For example, floor(1.9) = 1, floor(1.99) = 1, and floor(2) = 2 exactly, since 2 is already an integer. Floor functions are genuinely piecewise-constant: they hold one integer value across a whole stretch of inputs, then jump abruptly to the next integer right at each whole number.

Let's compute lim(x to 2-) floor(x). Restrict attention to inputs strictly less than 2 and let them close in on 2: x = 1.9 gives floor(1.9) = 1. x = 1.99 gives floor(1.99) = 1. x = 1.999 gives floor(1.999) = 1. In fact, for every x satisfying 1 <= x < 2, floor(x) = 1 exactly, with no variation at all. So as x approaches 2 from the left, the output does not just trend toward 1, it equals 1 the whole time once x is within that stretch. Therefore lim(x to 2-) floor(x) = 1.

This is worth contrasting with what would happen if you (incorrectly) plugged in x = 2 itself: floor(2) = 2, not 1. The left-hand limit is not asking for the value at 2; it is asking what the function is doing on the approach, strictly before arriving. For this particular function, the approach value (1) and the value at the point (2) are different, which is exactly the kind of behavior that makes floor functions a useful, if slightly extreme, teaching example.

For most familiar functions, the left-hand limit is no harder to find than any other limit, since there is no jump to worry about. For f(x) = 3x - 1 at a = 4, the left-hand limit lim(x to 4-) (3x - 1) can be found the same way as a two-sided limit, by substitution, because polynomials never jump: 3(4) - 1 = 11, and testing x = 3.9 gives 3(3.9) - 1 = 10.7, while x = 3.99 gives 10.97, both closing in on 11 as expected. The extra care one-sided notation demands really only earns its keep at breakpoints, domain edges, and jumps, exactly the kind of feature the floor function was chosen to illustrate.

Left-hand limits are computed with the same algebraic and numerical techniques as any other limit, factoring, simplifying, or tabulating, with the sole added restriction that every test input must stay below a. That restriction is small to write down but essential to respect, since including even one input at or above a would no longer describe "approaching from the left" at all, and would silently turn the calculation into a different, unrelated question.
